title: Why Mapmakers Put Fake Towns on Their Maps in the 1920s — and the One That Became Real
description: Open Cul­ture read­ers may know John Green best for Crash Course, the YouTube chan­nel that teach­es every­thing you need to know about sub­j
body:
Open Cul­ture read­ers may know John Green best for Crash Course, the YouTube chan­nel that teach­es every­thing you need to know about sub­jects like world his­to­ry, U.S. his­to­ry, big his­to­ry, lit­er­a­ture, and phi­los­o­phy. Or at least it teach­es every­thing a teenage stu­dent fac­ing down the prospect of Advanced Place­ment sub­ject exams needs to know. Such view­ers have always had a decent chance of know­ing Green as the author of nov­els for young read­ers like Look­ing for Alas­ka, The Fault in Our Stars, and Paper Towns. That last takes its title from just the kind of his­tor­i­cal phe­nom­e­non that would in any case have fas­ci­nat­ed Green, in his capac­i­ty as a vlog­ger, enough to inspire a video: the whol­ly fic­tion­al set­tle­ments cre­at­ed by map­mak­ers in order to expose car­to­graph­ic pla­gia­rists.

Green dis­cuss­es one such paper town in the episode of Vlog­broth­ers, the long-run­ning chan­nel Green runs with his broth­er Hank, at the top of the post. Agloe, New York, an upstate ham­let in Colch­ester, Delaware Coun­ty, was fab­ri­cat­ed in the nine­teen-twen­ties by car­tog­ra­ph­er Otto G. Lind­berg and his assis­tant Ernest Alpers, who’d been com­mis­sioned to make maps for the gas-sta­tion chain Esso.
Map­mak­ers (like Lind­berg and Alpers) have guard­ed against pla­gia­rism by insert­ing “paper towns” — invent­ed streets, land­marks, or oth­er fea­tures — into their maps. The log­ic is sim­ple: two car­tog­ra­phers might eas­i­ly draw the same real town, but two car­tog­ra­phers can’t inde­pen­dent­ly dream up the same fake one. So if a rival’s map con­tains the same invent­ed place, it all but proves they copied the map.
Though intend­ed as noth­ing more than a “copy­right trap,” the name of the dot in the road, Agloe, soon man­i­fest­ed in the real world. A busi­ness named Agloe Lodge Farms appeared in 1930, and it went on to apply the name to a local fish­ing lodge it acquired. Thus was Agloe, New York brought into exis­tence, at least in the eyes of the law: by the time they were chal­lenged about its inclu­sion on their own maps, Rand McNal­ly could cite offi­cial coun­ty records in their defense.

In oth­er words, “a made-up name for a made-up place inad­ver­tent­ly cre­at­ed a real place that, for a time, real­ly exist­ed,” writes NPR’s Robert Krul­wich. “Rand McNal­ly, one pre­sumes, was found not guilty. Then the store closed. It isn’t there any­more. Decades passed.” At the time Krul­wich was writ­ing, in 2014, an inter­net search for Agloe, New York would still return a point where Lind­berg and Alpers had orig­i­nal­ly placed it on their map the bet­ter part of a cen­tu­ry ear­li­er. “But then, just as this sto­ry was to be pub­lished, to be extra sure, we went to Google Earth, typed in ‘Agloe’ one last time, and, whad­dya know? It isn’t there any more!” Ado­les­cent read­ers imag­in­ing them­selves run­ning away in the man­ner of Mar­go Spiegel­man will have to seek out anoth­er far­away paper town to dream about — or, more like­ly these days, a pix­el town.

title: A Guide to Every Major Film Adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey Before Christopher Nolan’s Movie
description:
in Film, Literature, Television |   	July 30th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

If you plan on shoot­ing your own adap­ta­tion of Home­r’s Odyssey,
body:
in Film, Literature, Television |   	July 30th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

If you plan on shoot­ing your own adap­ta­tion of Home­r’s Odyssey, bear in mind how much rests on your choice of lead­ing man. In order to play Odysseus, an actor must sum­mon a real grav­i­tas, but also a still-smol­der­ing vital­i­ty: here is a man who led the Greek army to defeat Troy, but still has the dogged­ness to make the decade-long jour­ney back home to his wife. In the mid-nine­teen-fifties, Hol­ly­wood had just the chin for the job: Kirk Dou­glas, who plays Odysseus under his Latin name in the epony­mous Ulysses. Though mer­ci­less in its exci­sions to Home­r’s text, as explained in the Under­rat­ed Cin­e­ma video above, it still has more or less every­thing you’d want in a fan­tas­ti­cal Tech­ni­col­or spec­ta­cle — and one shot by The Wiz­ard of Oz vet­er­an Harold Rosson at that.

Those in search of a view­ing expe­ri­ence more adher­ent to the orig­i­nal sto­ry should con­sid­er L’Odis­sea: not the Ital­ian silent film from 1911 recent­ly fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture, but the 1968 Ital­ian minis­eries direct­ed by Fran­co Rossi, who would go on to be bet­ter known for Quo Vadis? Though no Odyssey adap­ta­tion fits every­thing in, this one gets just about as com­plete as a clas­sics fan could hope for in its 446-minute run­time.
As Odysseus, the Yugoslav heart­throb Bekim Fehmiu (for a brief moment there­after, cin­e­ma’s next glob­al star) may or may not be to your taste. More acclaimed is Armand Assante, por­tray­er of fig­ures from John Got­ti to Mick­ey Spillane to Niet­zsche, in NBC’s Odyssey minis­eries from 1997, which also fea­tures the likes of Isabel­la Rosselli­ni, Bernadette Peters, Christo­pher Lee, and Vanes­sa Williams.


	

Though star-stud­ded, shot in the real Mediter­ranean, and direct­ed by one­time Tarkovsky col­lab­o­ra­tor Andrei Kon­chalovsky, the Odyssey of the nineties isn’t much ref­er­enced today, per­haps due to its dat­ed visu­al effects. View­ers will nev­er have any such objec­tion to Uber­to Pasolin­i’s The Return, not because it only came out the year before last, but because it has prac­ti­cal­ly no visu­al effects in the first place. Focus­ing only on the lat­ter half of the Odyssey, the film dra­ma­tizes the reunion of Odysseus and his wife: a very human sto­ry, espe­cial­ly in that it con­tains no mon­sters. Dif­fer­ent adap­ta­tions have cut out the sirens, say, or Scyl­la and Charyb­dis, though it’s a rare pro­duc­tion bold enough not to put every­thing it has into the cyclops scene. But you can get an actor like Ralph Fiennes to play Odysseus — and for that mat­ter, Juli­ette Binoche to play Pene­lope — there’s lit­tle need for a crea­ture fea­ture.

title: The Visionary Mystical Art of Carl Jung: See Illustrated Pages from The Red Book
description: Carl Jung’s Liber Novus, bet­ter known as The Red Book, has come to light in a com­plete Eng­lish trans­la­tion, pub­lished by Nor­ton in a 2009
body:
Carl Jung’s Liber Novus, bet­ter known as The Red Book, has come to light in a com­plete Eng­lish trans­la­tion, pub­lished by Nor­ton in a 2009 fac­sim­i­le edi­tion and a small­er “reader’s edi­tion” in 2012. The years since have seen sev­er­al exhi­bi­tions of the book, which “could pass for a Bible ren­dered by a medieval monk,” writes art crit­ic Peter Frank, “espe­cial­ly for the care with which Jung entered his writ­ing as ornate Goth­ic script.”
Jung “refused to think of him­self as an ‘artist’” but “it’s no acci­dent the Liber Novus has been exhib­it­ed in muse­ums, or func­tioned as the nucle­us of ‘Ency­clo­pe­dic Palace,’ the sur­vey of vision­ary art in the 2013 Venice Bien­nale.” Jung’s elab­o­rate paint­ings show him “every bit the artist the medieval monk or Per­sian courtier was; his art hap­pened to be ded­i­cat­ed not to the glo­ry of God or king, but that of the human race.”
One could more accu­rate­ly say that Jung’s book was ded­i­cat­ed to the mys­ti­cal uncon­scious, a much more neb­u­lous and ocean­ic cat­e­go­ry. The “ocean­ic feeling”—a phrase coined in 1927 by French play­wright Romain Rol­land to describe mys­ti­cal oneness—so annoyed Sig­mund Freud that he dis­missed it as infan­tile regres­sion.

Freud’s antipa­thy to mys­ti­cism, as we know, did not dis­suade Jung, his one­time stu­dent and admir­er, from div­ing in and swim­ming to the deep­est depths. The voy­age began long before he met his famous men­tor. At age 11, Jung lat­er wrote in 1959, “I found that I had been in a mist, not know­ing how to dif­fer­en­ti­ate myself from things; I was just one among many things.”


	

Jung con­sid­ered his elab­o­rate dream/vision journal—kept from 1913 to 1930, then added to spo­rad­i­cal­ly until 1961—“the cen­tral work in his oeu­vre,” says Jung schol­ar Sonu Sham­dasani in the Rubin Muse­um intro­duc­tion above. “It is lit­er­al­ly his most impor­tant work.”
And yet it took Dr. Sham­dasani “three years to con­vince Jung’s fam­i­ly to bring the book out of hid­ing,” notes NPR. “It took anoth­er 13 years to trans­late it.” Part of the rea­son his heirs left the book hid­den in a Swiss vault for half a cen­tu­ry may be evi­dent in the only por­tion of the Red Book to appear in Jung’s life­time, “The Sev­en Ser­mons of the Dead.”

Jung had this text pri­vate­ly print­ed in 1916 and gave copies to select friends and fam­i­ly mem­bers. He com­posed it in 1913 in a peri­od of Gnos­tic stud­ies, dur­ing which he entered into vision­ary trance states, tran­scrib­ing his visions in note­books called the “Black Books,” which would lat­er be rewrit­ten in The Red Book.
You can see a page of Jung’s metic­u­lous­ly hand-let­tered man­u­script above. The “Ser­mons,” he wrote in a lat­er inter­pre­ta­tion, came to him dur­ing an actu­al haunt­ing:
The atmos­phere was thick, believe me! Then I knew that some­thing had to hap­pen. The whole house was filled as if there were a crowd present, crammed full of spir­its. They were packed deep right up to the door, and the air was so thick it was scarce­ly pos­si­ble to breathe. As for myself, I was all a‑quiver with the ques­tion: “For God’s sake, what in the world is this?” Then they cried out in cho­rus, “We have come back from Jerusalem where we found not what we sought/’ That is the begin­ning of the Septem Ser­mones. 
The strange, short “ser­mons” are dif­fi­cult to cat­e­go­rize. They are awash in Gnos­tic the­ol­o­gy and occult terms like “plero­ma.” The great mys­ti­cal one­ness of ocean­ic feel­ing also took on a very sin­is­ter aspect in the demigod Abraxas, who “beget­teth truth and lying, good and evil, light and dark­ness, in the same word and in the same act. Where­fore is Abraxas ter­ri­ble.”

There are tedious, didac­tic pas­sages, for con­verts only, but much of Jung’s writ­ing in the “Sev­en Ser­mons,” and through­out The Red Book, is filled with strange obscure poet­ry, com­ple­ment­ed by his intense illus­tra­tions. Jung “took on the sim­i­lar­ly styl­ized and beau­ti­ful man­ners of non-west­ern word-image con­fla­tion,” writes Frank, “includ­ing Per­sian minia­ture paint­ing and east Asian cal­lig­ra­phy.”
If The Red Book is, as Sham­dasani claims, Jung’s most impor­tant work—and Jung him­self, though he kept it qui­et, seemed to think it was—then we may in time come to think of him not only as an inspir­er of eccen­tric artists, but as an eccen­tric artist him­self, on par with the great illu­mi­na­tors and vision­ary mys­tic poet/painters.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2020.

body:
“Blue Jay.” All images courtesy of The Paper Ark, shared with permission
July 30, 2026
ArtNature
Kate Mothes

From meticulously cut and painted pieces of paper, realistic birds emerge amid foliage and forests in compositions by The Paper Ark. The collaborative practice of Nayan Shrimali and Venus Bird, which focuses on intricate paper reliefs, also centers on ecology by illustrating real species and their habitats around the world. The duo aims to raise awareness of biodiversity and conservation by evoking a sense of wonder akin to how we also often feel in nature.
The artists recently exhibited a number of the pieces shown here with Antler Gallery at Seattle Art Fair, and “Great Green Macaws” appeared in the Spring 2026 issue of Audubon Magazine. See more on The Paper Ark’s Instagram.

title: Reflections Dazzle in the Hyperrealistic Chrome Faces of Kip Omolade's Vivid Portraits
description: Set against uninterrupted backgrounds, the bold, metallic portraits of Kip Omolade float almost deity-like amid vibrant color. Known for his hyper
body:
Set against uninterrupted backgrounds, the bold, metallic portraits of Kip Omolade float almost deity-like amid vibrant color. Known for his hyperrealistic treatment of chrome-like visages in oil paint, the artist sometimes incorporates spray-painted elements, drawing on the graffiti culture of New York City’s subways during the 1980s and 1990s when Omolade tagged using the moniker “Kace.”
The artist also presents the mask-like faces from different vantage points, sometimes with incredible eyelashes, whether peering directly at the viewer or positioned in regal profile. Reflections are typically abstract, showing little indication of the surrounding space beyond perhaps blue skies, the sun, and local color, although the monumental “African History” is an exception.
“Diovadiova Chrome Karyn XXII”
Upon closer inspection, the whorls of “African History” reveal numerous additional faces inspired by a wide range of carved sculptures the artist observed in a long-running exhibition at The Metropolitan Museum of Art titled The African Origin of Civilization, plus other examples from art history. Within this one, larger-than-life identity is a host of time-honored traditions and creative expressions.

title: The Top Photos in the CWAS David Malin Awards Highlight Astronomical Wonders
description: Every year, the Central West Astronomical Society (CWAS) of New South Wales celebrates AstroFest, a festival of astronomy during which amateur pho
body:
Every year, the Central West Astronomical Society (CWAS) of New South Wales celebrates AstroFest, a festival of astronomy during which amateur photographers and scientists from around the globe are invited to submit their best views of the night sky and beyond. This year, the overall prize was awarded to Stefan Buda for his tonal moonscape titled “The Lunar Apennines,” which captures a detailed view of Montes Apenninus.
Categories include Deep Sky, Solar System, Wide-Field, Nightscapes, and more, allowing photographers to contribute images of phenomena ranging from distant nebulae and spiral galaxies to the Milky Way and aurora australis, or the southern lights, shining above impressive terrestrial landscapes. A 2027 calendar featuring the winning images is available for purchase, and you can see the entire gallery of top shots on the award’s website.
Stefan Buda, “The Lunar Apennines.” Overall winner of the CWAS David Malin Award and winner of the Solar System category
Andy Campbell, “OED1 – Winged Sandals of Mercury.” Honorable mention in the Deep Sky category

title: Janice Yang's Symbol-Rich Paintings Conjure Dreams and the Desire for Home
description: At the age of 14, Janice Yang and her family emigrated from South Korea to the U.S. in the wake of a financial crisis that upended their sense of
body:
At the age of 14, Janice Yang and her family emigrated from South Korea to the U.S. in the wake of a financial crisis that upended their sense of security. (Incidentally, the Korean stock market is experiencing a historic crash this month in the wake of unwinding global trade in the AI sector.) Displaced from everything they knew, her family had to start again. “Our stable economic situation in Korea changed to more precarious working-class reality in the U.S., where repeated business failures left us in a lot of debt,” Yang tells Colossal.
For two decades, Yang worked unpaid at her family’s small sushi restaurant, where she dreamed of eventually pursuing her studies to become an artist, all while navigating a new culture and helping to carry her family’s financial burden. “These years of labor and adaptation have profoundly shaped my identity as a first-generation immigrant and my artistic practice,” she says. Her figurative paintings, which often center self-portraits amid busy kitchens, are accompanied by dream-like clouds and distant vistas that open up in walls and windows or float around the figures’ heads. There’s also a lot of fish.
“The Hours Between (노을의 색들)” (2026), salmon ash and oil on canvas, 48 x 60 inches
Whether filleted, whole, chopped, or cooking, salmon are prevalent in many of Yang’s compositions. In a sense, they were the artist’s constant companions for years. “Every day, I saw salmon getting flayed and prepped in plastic wrap to be stored into the fridge,” she says. “I would develop personal feelings to salmon and personify them, since they reminded me the unfulfilled dream I had as an artist.” They also represent the desire to return home.
Every year, salmon complete the physically demanding biological process of spawning, in which they migrate from the ocean to their native freshwater streams and rivers to lay eggs. Huge numbers of the fish home in on the place they were born, fighting their way upstream to ensure the survival of the next generation. “This related to my feelings and hopes to reach my dream and find the sense of belonging in a new place where I felt often lost,” Yang says. Occasionally, her paintings incorporate salmon ash along with acrylic and oil pigments.
The artist also nods to symbolic elements of Korean art history and visual culture, such as a scroll painting by Ahn Gyeon, a court painter during Joseon Dynasty in the 15th century. The unfurled work sits on the lap of the figure in “Ahn Gyeon’s Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land.” The painting is now held in a collection in Japan, and Yang describes how Koreans hope to see the painting returned to its homeland someday. Korean aesthetics converge with classical Western artistic methods like one-point perspective. Yang says, “For me, this blending of visual languages becomes a way to think through ideas of home, coexistence, and contradiction, and to reflect on the complexity of diasporic identity.”
Starting next month, Yang will be an artist-in-residence at Gallery MOMO in Johannesburg, South Africa, where she will also present an exhibition. And in September, she will commence a nine-month artist residency at Lillstreet Art Center in Chicago, where she will teach, in addition to being a visiting lecturer at the School of the Art Institute’s Painting and Drawing Department. See more on Yang’s Instagram.
